tldr: Unfastening screws requires millimeter-level alignment and delicate force execution. By dividing the process into two stages—alignment & insertion, and unfastening—and combining a multi-modal diffusion model with stage transition detection, this framework autonomously performs screw removal on a real robot.
hero_caption: An overview of the hierarchical framework, DAWN. Integrating multi-camera images, proprioception (robot end-effector poses), and force sensor readings, it handles everything end-to-end on a real robot: from millimeter-level alignment and insertion using an electric screwdriver to unfastening screws.
overview:
In recycling and reverse engineering of household appliances and electric vehicle batteries, disassembly is an essential process. Within disassembly, unfastening fasteners accounts for roughly 40% to 60% of total disassembly time. Yet, it still relies almost entirely on manual human labor. Automating it with robots has been extremely challenging because it demands engaging the screwdriver tip with sub-millimeter precision, controlling forces carefully to avoid stripping screws or damaging the robot arm, and maintaining robustness against background and lighting variations.

Instead of solving the entire task with a single end-to-end model, the authors propose DAWN (Diffusion-based Alignment and unfastening Workflow Network), a hierarchical framework that splits the task into two sequential stages: "alignment & insertion" and "unfastening." It coordinates three specialized networks: AlignNet, which uses multi-modal representations and a diffusion model for positioning and insertion; LatchNet, which accurately detects screw engagement using vision and force; and UnfastNet, which achieves stable, low-latency, force-controlled screw removal while safely venting reaction torques.

Equipping a Franka Emika robot with a custom electric screwdriver, the team performed extensive real-robot trials totaling nearly 1,000 runs. AlignNet achieved an insertion success rate of 50% ± 8.3%, matching trained human operators. Furthermore, combining LatchNet for phase transitions and UnfastNet for screw removal demonstrated strong generalization across diverse unseen screws and bolts, achieving stable task execution.
contributions: Proposed and demonstrated DAWN, the first learning-based hierarchical control framework for high-precision, contact-rich unfastening tasks in real-world environments.

Achieved an insertion success rate on par with trained human operators using AlignNet, which integrates vision, force, and proprioception via a transformer decoder and generates high-precision trajectories with a diffusion model.
Constructed a reliable phase transition mechanism using LatchNet, a binary classifier fusing vision and force to verify that the screwdriver bit has securely engaged the screw head.
Demonstrated 100% unfastening success on unseen screws and bolts using UnfastNet, which leverages force feedback and heuristic safety constraints for high generalization.

sections.heading: Why is automating unfastening so difficult?
sections.summary: Unfastening accounts for most disassembly time, requiring millimeter-level positioning and precise contact force control. This section outlines the limitations of existing vision detectors and monolithic learning models, explaining why DAWN splits the workflow into two sequential stages and solves them multi-modally.
sections.details:
With growing volumes of electronic waste and end-of-life EV batteries, automating recycling facilities has become an urgent need. Unfastening fasteners makes up 39.9% to 60% of product disassembly time. Automating this step could significantly lower operational costs and improve worker safety.

However, deploying robots for real-world unfastening faces three major hurdles:
- First, the accuracy limits of vision-based fastener detection and 3D coordinate transformation. Glare, lighting variations, and cluttered backgrounds introduce noise, making it difficult to locate the exact center of a screw head at the millimeter level purely from image recognition.
- Second, strict tolerances for positional error and force control. Engaging a screwdriver bit with a screw head requires sub-millimeter alignment. Excessive downward force can strip screw threads or damage the robot arm, while insufficient force causes the bit to slip off.
- Third, the long task horizon. Unfastening is a contact-rich sequence: approaching the target, aligning precisely, inserting, and rotating while loosening. Attempting to solve this entire sequence with a single policy leads to compounding errors and task failure.

To overcome these hurdles, the authors clearly divided the process into two stages: (1) alignment & insertion, and (2) unfastening. They designed DAWN, a hierarchical framework comprising AlignNet for precise guidance, LatchNet for detecting engagement to switch stages, and UnfastNet for safe screw loosening.

sections.heading: Existing automated unfastening and the current state of imitation learning
sections.summary: Previous unfastening studies depended on custom hardware or simple computer vision, leaving them vulnerable to real-world variations. Meanwhile, for long-horizon contact-rich imitation learning challenges like distributional shift, diffusion models and multi-modal integration have emerged as promising solutions.
sections.details:
This section reviews prior work on unfastening automation and recent trends in imitation learning (IL) for contact-rich manipulation.

### II-A Unfastening Task
Previous unfastening research focused primarily on deep-learning-based screw detection and pose estimation, or on specialized tooling tailored to hexagonal bolts. However, mapping detected coordinates into 3D physical space introduced substantial errors, and most methods still required humans to provide exact fastener coordinates beforehand. Additionally, experiments were often limited to specific electronics like hard drives or laptops, leaving robustness against environmental variations and contact force control largely unaddressed.

### II-B Imitation learning
When tackling long-horizon contact tasks through policy learning, reinforcement learning (RL) suffers from difficult reward engineering and the massive number of real-world interactions required. On the other hand, imitation learning (IL) directly learns from human teleoperation demonstrations, but compounding prediction errors over time—known as distributional shift—remain a major challenge. Recently, Diffusion Policy, capable of smoothly capturing multi-modal action distributions, alongside multi-modal fusion combining vision, touch, and force, has dramatically boosted manipulation robustness. This paper applies the strengths of multi-modal diffusion models to the extremely delicate unfastening task.

sections.heading: The three-network architecture of DAWN
sections.summary: DAWN consists of three modules: AlignNet (diffusion model for end-effector trajectories), LatchNet (binary classifier for stage transitions), and UnfastNet (lightweight MLP for force-controlled loosening). Multi-modal integration via a transformer decoder and smooth control via action chunking form its core.
sections.details:
DAWN's training and inference pipeline combines high-quality teleoperated demonstration collection with three specialized networks tailored to specific roles.

### III-A Teleoperation, Data Collection and Pre-processing
The experimental platform uses a Franka Emika 7-DoF robot with built-in force/torque sensing, fitted with a custom electric screwdriver facing vertically downward at the end-effector. A human operator controls the robot end-effector at 10 Hz using an Xbox controller to collect demonstrations. Observations include RGB images from three RealSense cameras (wrist-mounted, front, and right side), end-effector and tool tip poses, end-effector positions, and force sensor readings. All observations are normalized to $[-1, 1]$.

### III-B Model Architecture
The system is divided into three distinct modules, each trained independently:

- **AlignNet (Alignment & Insertion)**:
  Vision (wrist camera images), proprioception (3D end-effector coordinates), and force readings are encoded into 256-dimensional feature vectors using dedicated encoders (ResNet-18 with GroupNorm or MLPs). These representations, along with a learnable Action Token, are passed to a transformer decoder termed the "Observation Trunk" to model inter-modality dependencies and generate a comprehensive context representation. Conditioned on this context, a 1D Temporal CNN-based diffusion model (DDPM) generates future absolute end-effector position trajectories of horizon $T_p=16$. During inference, action chunking executes the first $T_a=8$ steps alongside exponential time ensembling, ensuring smooth and stable approach and insertion.

- **LatchNet (Stage Transition Detection)**:
  A binary classifier that determines whether the screwdriver bit has successfully latched into the screw head. An ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18 with frozen weights encodes wrist camera images, which are concatenated with force readings encoded by a 2-layer MLP, and passed through a sigmoid function to output 0 or 1. It is trained using binary cross-entropy loss.

- **UnfastNet (Unfastening)**:
  During the active unfastening phase, using heavy generative models like diffusion policies introduces computational latency, frequently triggering safety stops when reaction forces spike. Therefore, UnfastNet adopts a lightweight 3-layer MLP. Taking force sensor values as input, it predicts relative positional offsets (delta actions) from the current pose. In addition, it incorporates heuristic safety constraints: limiting end-effector reaction force to under 20 N, and automatically stopping screwdriver rotation the moment contact force reaches 10 N or higher.

sections.heading: Insights and performance across 1,000 real-robot trials
sections.summary: Using a Franka Emika robot, nearly 1,000 real-world trials were conducted. AlignNet achieved insertion success rates matching trained human operators, and UnfastNet achieved a 100% success rate across diverse unseen fasteners. However, limitations regarding visual occlusion and low contrast also emerged.
sections.details:
Evaluations were conducted on a workstation with an NVIDIA RTX 4080 and the real Franka Emika robot, spanning roughly 1,000 total rollouts. Analysis focused heavily on "alignment & insertion," which serves as the primary bottleneck of the entire workflow.

### IV-A Task Description
Phillips screws were placed randomly on a box within a 40 cm $\times$ 15 cm workspace. Rollouts were categorized and analyzed using strictly defined evaluation stages: "Alignment" (vertically aligned over the axis), "Proximity" (within a 2 cm radius), "Insertion" (beginning descent after proximity), and "Success" (fully engaged and latched).

### IV-B Capability of DAWN to Learn
- **AlignNet**: Under a strict 4 mm tolerance, AlignNet achieved a $50\% \pm 8.3\%$ success rate. This matches trained, skilled human operators (50%–60%) and significantly outperforms novice humans (20%). Furthermore, training the visual encoder from scratch yielded better performance than fine-tuning from ImageNet pre-training.
- **LatchNet**: Achieved high classification performance with an accuracy of 0.90, precision of 0.90, recall of 0.98, and an F1-score of 0.94. The high recall is especially critical: it ensures false positives (advancing to unfastening without engagement) are near zero, preventing robot arm damage.
- **UnfastNet**: While diffusion policies triggered frequent safety halts due to latency and force spikes, the combination of a lightweight MLP and force-based safety heuristics achieved exceptionally stable unfastening.

### IV-C Impact of Modalities on Performance
Ablations revealed key modality insights. For AlignNet, wrist camera images combined with proprioception alone yielded top performance; adding front camera or force inputs only increased computation without improving accuracy. In contrast, LatchNet required both vision and force: vision alone was vulnerable to occlusion, while force alone mistook accidental collisions for latching. UnfastNet relied exclusively on force data, granting it environmental invariance against background shifts.

### IV-D Generalization and Robustness
Generalization was tested across unseen fasteners and materials. UnfastNet maintained a 100% unfastening success rate across varying screw diameters, lengths, and materials. However, for AlignNet, smaller screws allowed proximity within 2 cm but caused failures during final insertion. Low-contrast backgrounds (like wood) prevented even alignment. With hex bolts, the socket bit completely occluded the bolt head, eliminating visual feedback and degrading latch detection.

### IV-E & IV-F Complete Unfastening Task & Ablation
Performance improved steadily as demonstration counts increased, and the Observation Trunk (transformer decoder) proved crucial for balancing positional representations. The complete end-to-end task success rate was $5.0\% \pm 0.8\%$ (noting 5 successes out of 10 trials). Once the bit latched successfully into the screw head, subsequent unfastening succeeded with 100% reliability.

sections.heading: Conclusion and future outlook
sections.summary: DAWN demonstrates that a hierarchical approach can autonomously perform challenging real-world unfastening tasks. Looking forward, handling visual occlusion and adapting to low-contrast backgrounds represent the primary hurdles to full practical deployment.
sections.details:
This work proposed DAWN, a hierarchical multi-modal imitation learning framework addressing unfastening, a vital task for automated recycling.

By decoupling the task into "alignment & insertion" and "unfastening," and assigning dedicated networks suited to each physical regime (a diffusion model, a binary classifier, and a force-controlled MLP), DAWN achieved human-level alignment accuracy and reliable unfastening across various fasteners.

Nevertheless, clear limitations remain before practical deployment. First, AlignNet degrades when confronted with visual appearances far outside its training data, such as low-contrast wooden backgrounds or tiny screws. Second, when tools completely occlude the fastener—as with hex bolts—visual information is lost, breaking latch detection. Future work points toward rich data augmentations, proximity sensors on the bit, or advanced tactile sensing to reduce over-reliance on purely visual contact detection.

takeaways: For contact-rich, long-horizon manipulation, modularizing the architecture according to the bandwidth and control mode needed in each phase is far more effective than forcing a single end-to-end model.

While diffusion models excel at high-precision trajectory alignment (AlignNet), their inference latency makes lightweight MLPs with force-based safety constraints better suited for contact tasks with reactive forces (UnfastNet).
Fusing vision (spatial awareness) and force (contact confirmation), as in LatchNet, drastically reduces misclassifications that cannot be prevented by either modality alone.
Imitation learning policies relying heavily on cameras remain vulnerable to physical tool occlusion and low background contrast, making tactile and auxiliary sensing key areas for future integration.
limitations: AlignNet alignment accuracy drops significantly when encountering fastener sizes different from training or low-contrast backgrounds like wood surfaces.
For fasteners such as bolts where the tool tip completely envelops the head, vision-based engagement detection (LatchNet) fails due to severe visual occlusion.
The setup assumes fastener heads are oriented parallel to the workspace surface (pointing vertically upward); handling fasteners driven in at oblique angles remains unverified.
